name: Hyatt
headline: A hotel brand that collects fees from owners and has grown its room count fast.
what_it_does: Hyatt licenses its hotel brands and manages hotels for owners, collecting fees as a share of hotel revenue under long contracts, along with a reservation and loyalty system. It has sold most of the hotels it used to own. The system had 373,000 rooms at the end of 2025, up from 223,000 in 2019.
why_it_passed: Its fee system needs little of its own capital, and the room count grew about 8.9% a year from 2019 to 2025, faster than Marriott (4.3%) or Hilton (5.6%).
Fees are paid as a share of hotel revenue under long contracts, so revenue is steadier than the hotel business itself.
Gross fees almost doubled from $608 million in 2019 to $1,198 million in 2025, though part of that came from acquisitions.
It has a pipeline of about 148,000 more rooms.
why_not_now: The price was $162.92. The analysis's central value range is about -$3 to $40 a share, and even a more generous version tops out at $125. A buyer at that price would earn only about 2% a year on the cash produced, against 5.56% on a 30-year US Treasury bond.
watch: It spent $5.1 billion on acquisitions in five years (mostly offset by hotel sales), yet cash left for owners did not rise.
It pays 12.8% of gross fees as incentive payments to win and keep hotel contracts, double what Marriott and Hilton pay.
The cash left for owners is only about 7% of gross fees, against 44% at Marriott and 51% at Hilton, and online platforms and short-term rentals are a named threat.
